newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand rocks markets with baht flotation.
newsitem.headline: Thailand rocks markets with baht flotation.

text.p: Thailand floated the baht and raised its key lending rate by two percentage points on Wednesday in a desperate attempt to put the fire back in its battered economy.

But currency analysts, who initially interpreted the move as a de facto devaluation which would allow the central bank to avoid costly intervention, said they would wait and see how far the baht would be allowed to fall.
The news, which sent shock waves through Southeast Asian markets, knocked 20 percent off the value of the baht and sent the currency to a record quoted low of 29.25 to the dollar, from 24.25 earlier.
At 0800 GMT the baht was trading at 28.30/90 to the dollar. Analysts said the currency could weaken further to 30.00 to the dollar.

The baht flotation caused the Japanese yen to rise against the U.S. dollar on safe-haven buying to a day's high of 114.15 yen, but the dollar later trimmed its losses and was quoted at about 114.50 yen at 0805 GMT.
"The value of the baht will be determined by market forces to reflect fundamental economic forces," finance minister Thanong Bidaya said in an early morning statement.
"The Ministry of Finance and the Bank of Thailand believe the managed float system will benefit Thailand's overall economic development," he said.
Thailand's stock market gave a hearty thumbs-up to the news, and investors boosted the index for the bourse by nearly eight percent in busy trade. Business was dominated by foreign institutions.

"There was a tremendous buildup of funds that were waiting to go into the market if there was a devaluation or, as it happened, a flotation," George Morgan, country manager for ABN Amro Hoare Govett, told Reuters Financial Television.
In a bid to keep the baht from a meltdown, the Bank of Thailand simultaneously raised its key commercial bank lending rate by two percentage points to 12.5 percent.

But commercial banks would not quote overnight lending rates and exchange trade ground to a virtual halt as markets waited for the central bank to announce its new baht reference rate, due at around 1000 GMT.
The rate will replace the previous daily peg, which was fixed against a trade-weighted basket of currencies dominated by the U.S. dollar.
The Bank of Thailand said it had "an appropriate rate" in mind in which it expected the baht to move, but gave no details.
"However, if the baht goes beyond the approriate rate the central bank will intervene in the market," central bank governor Chaiyawat Wibulsawasdi told a news conference.
Analysts said there was a question-mark over how far and how fast the central would allow the baht to fall, but they expected it to bring the currency down gradually.
They said that in the near-term, higher interest rates would hurt Thailand's economy, which is still grappling with a swollen current account deficit, slowing growth, and a troubled financial sector.
But analysts said that if the new measures did ultimately restore confidence, there would be scope for Thai interest rates to fall in the coming months.

The flotation will also allow the Bank of Thailand to avoid intervening to support the baht. The bank used up to five billion dollars of its foreign reserves in May to defend the currency after it came under heavy attack.
This cut the country's foreign reserves to a two-year low of $33.3 billion at the end of May from around $37.3 billion a month earlier

"Clearly their backs were to the wall given the speculative attack on the baht and I think these measures are aimed at boosting confidence," said Kobus van der Watch, Regional Head of Treasury and Economics at Standard Chartered in Singapore.
"But fixing a reference point for the bath allows them to set the pace," he said.
Analysts had expected renewed near-term speculation against the baht because of negative sentiment over the Thai economy and recent moves to rescue its beleaguered financial institutions.
"Under the new system movements in the exchange rate are expected to be quite large at the initial stage. However, relative stability should be attained after a brief adjustment period," Bidaya said.
The news hit regional stock and money markets, with several governments reacting quickly to offset any negative impact.

The Philippines sold hundreds of millions of dollars and forced up interest rates to shield its currency. Manila stocks fell to close nearly two percent lower on Wednesday as stock market investors took fright.
For the first time in years, Bank Negara Malaysia used its own name to intervene in the foreign exchange market as it sold dollars early on Wednesday.
The Indonesian rupiah also slipped lower, while in Japan, the yen gained against major currencies on its safe-haven status in the region.
The Bank of Japan welcomed the decision and said the baht's flotation increased the scope for cooperation among central banks.
In Australia, the Reserve Bank confirmed it had been asked to provide technical advice to the Bank of Thailand for the managed float, but gave no details.
Thailand said it had also asked the International Monetary Fund for technical help.
